title: What will you leave?
hookLine: a well, a book, a child's prayer

cards: A well, dug in hot ground, still giving water long after the man who paid for it is gone. A book, copied and recopied, still read by people who will never meet its author.
A child, grown now, raising her hands after the prayer to ask mercy for a parent who died years ago. None of them is a building with a name on it, or a fortune, or a title.
Yet a saying of the Prophet ﷺ names exactly these three as the things that keep working after a life ends.

teach.h: WHEN A PERSON DIES, THREE THINGS GO ON.
SADAQA JARIYA: CHARITY THAT RUNS LIKE WATER.
teach.b: In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end except for three: a charity that keeps on flowing, knowledge that others benefit from, and a righteous child who prays for them.
Three doors left open after the house is closed. Second, the flowing charity. Its Arabic name is sadaqa jariya.

Abu Dawud keeps a story about a companion, Sa'd ibn Ubada, whose mother had died. He asked the Prophet which charity was best, and the answer was water. So Sa'd dug a well and said it was for his mother.
A report in Tirmidhi also tells of a well in Medina that Uthman bought so people could draw from it freely. Water, given once, keeps giving. Third, the knowledge.
This whole year has been full of it: scholars who wrote, teachers who taught a single student who taught another.
A lesson passed on keeps working in someone else's life, whether or not anyone remembers who taught it first.

teach.h: A RIGHTEOUS CHILD WHO PRAYS FOR THEM.
teach.b: Fourth, the child's prayer: in the hadith's words, a righteous child who prays for the parent, a son or a daughter asking mercy by name after the prayer. Then notice what's missing from the list: wealth and power.
A well can be a share in one. Knowledge can be one skill taught well.

teach.h: WHAT THEY SENT AHEAD, AND THE TRACES THEY LEFT.
teach.b: And the Qur'an widens the frame, in a verse that speaks of a record of what people sent ahead and the traces they left behind.

how: Muslims give sadaqa jariya in forms such as funding wells, mosques, schools, copies of the Qur'an or trees, often on behalf of parents who have died, and children make du'a for their parents after prayer.

o: a charity that keeps flowing after you die
a gift given in secret, without your name
the yearly alms owed on a person's savings

games.q: what will you leave — tap the pairs.
p: dug a well for his mother
bought a well for people to use freely
prays for a parent after death

s: the hadith says deeds end at death except for three things
a flowing charity, beneficial knowledge, and a righteous child who prays.
only the wealthy can leave sadaqa jariya
a share in a well or one skill taught well can carry on; none of the three needs a fortune.
when Sa'd asked which charity was best, he was told to build a mosque
the answer was water, so he dug a well for his mother.

games.q: you are Sa'd ibn Ubada. your mother has died, and you want to give charity for her. you ask the Prophet which charity is best. what does he say?
games.why: he said water. Sa'd dug a well and said it was for his mother. in a hot land, water given once keeps giving.

practice: Look at the three doors: something that keeps giving, like water, a book for a library, a tree, a scholarship or a ramp; one thing you know that someone younger needs, a recipe, a skill, how to pray, how to fix a bike; or a child in your life you could be more present for.
Choose one door and picture the smallest first step. If you pray, you can ask Allah to accept it; if not, simply hold the plan.

wordCard.voice: Sadaqa jariya, a flowing charity like a well that keeps giving water long after the person who paid for it is gone. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: flowing charity, a good that keeps working after the giver has died.

carryVoice: Your line: three doors left open. None of them needs a fortune. That's today, done.
